doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Audience, the 'Stage & Screen' record and keeping fans while changing repertoire
summary: Prompted by the question of audience, he talks about songs of the 1960s to 80s, how jazz listeners changed, and avoiding an all-new-album show.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: A few years ago my wife and I wrote a book based on these interviews and the publisher said, “Well first we want to know who’s your audience?” And for some reason I got a little annoyed with the question. I mean like well jazz people. I mean have you ever had a record label say that to you? Like who’s your audience? And should you do any adjustment of your song list and etcetera.

Well you know I try to make, I have a record that I’m trying to finish up of songs again from ‘60s, ‘70s, and ‘80s. I continually have these things because and I say I just made this “Stage & Screen” record and I really feel like we finally communicated what we do. It only took me, you know 33 years to sit on the stage and go oh, “Too Close for Comfort” and that, and feel like people are getting it. You know really on a wider stage than just say jazz people. I just felt like this is something that’s unique, how we’re going about this, or at least we’re carrying on a tradition in a really great way. And yet the people who are my age would know the songs from the ‘60s and ‘70s. We all grew up with this music and I think the other thing that’s sort of interesting is when I was twenty, with Bucky, there were the jazz listeners. They were their own group. They were maybe Bucky’s age. But they didn’t have The Beatles. They had Count Basie and Oscar Peterson and that music, Sinatra. It was a specific group I think. And as I got older there were the people who were my age who were brought up with their parents playing those things and starting to go oh — and then you had Diana Krall and Natalie Cole and Harry Connick singing standards on the radio in the ‘90s and everybody going oh this was a new thing. It was like hip to know “It Had to be You” all of a sudden, to sing “Unforgettable.” So I’m leaving out a completely different thing I was going to say. But so the hardest thing is thinking about can we sell records playing jazz of more recent songs and still communicate to those people who like “Too Close for Comfort” and “As Time Goes By” and those things. So that’s always the challenge like I want to go okay. And my manager seems to think oh no, they’ll follow you. Your people will follow you. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

They want to know what you have to say. And they have, they’ve followed me through the Beatle record and through “Double Exposure” and the bossa nova records and tours of those things. I think the thing is not to make it a complete show. I would still say you’ve still got to play something here, something there, and in the middle you can promote the new album but I think it’s still like as opposed to making it an entire evening of one thing.
